中高齡女性開始重訓：加蛋白質、加肌酸或加有氧，如何判斷下一步？ 
力量、肌肉量與心肺適能需要不同證據。以中高齡女性訓練與蛋白質試驗，對照成人肌酸統合分析，本專題建立「先確認訓練刺激與飲食，再評估營養加成」的執行流程，釐清未檢出差異、體組成估計及女性證據不足的決策邊界。 
training 
nutrition 
assessment 
monitoring 
對剛開始阻力訓練、以增加力量為主要目標的中高齡女性，何時應先調整訓練與飲食執行，何時才值得討論提高蛋白質或加入肌酸？ 
兩篇全文回答不同但相連的問題：女性隨機試驗比較阻力訓練後增加騎車，以及不同蛋白質目標的飲食諮詢；肌酸統合分析比較阻力訓練加肌酸與加安慰劑。可以整合成決策流程，不能將兩篇效果值直接排名，也不能推論肌酸優於蛋白質，或能抵銷新增有氧後的力量差距。已依所附全文、表格、圖說、討論及限制判讀；未附的補充檔不視為已核閱。 
封包中的 2026 年 9 月肌酸研究與 ACSM 女性能量平衡更新，使「營養如何支持訓練」成為適合深入說明的問題。更新題名只提供時效背景；效果與數值全部取自本期選定全文。 
第 39 週已介紹新增騎車的結果取捨，第 40 週已介紹肌酸平均效益；仍缺少以中高齡女性為主體、能區分訓練不足、飲食未落實與可考慮補充情境的完整流程。尤其女性試驗的蛋白質不顯著結果，容易被誤讀成不必重視蛋白質。 
當力量進步不如預期，團隊需決定要維持方案、調整新增騎車、修正飲食，或另行試用肌酸；同時避免以 BIA 肌肉量上升、體脂率下降或補充品用量，代替真正的能力結果。 
區分力量表現、BIA 骨骼肌量、瘦體重與體脂率，說明各自能支持的結論。 
讀懂第 12 週調整後組間差、Hedges’ g、信賴區間與預測區間。 
說明蛋白質指派目標未檢出差異，為何不代表三種攝取量等效。 
辨認成人肌酸整合結果外推到中高齡女性時的限制。 
完成包含基線、分期課表、飲食紀錄、選擇性補充、進退階與複評責任人的執行方案。 
先問希望改善哪個結果，再問目前實際做了什麼。肌肉量是組織或儀器估計，力量是完成特定任務的能力，有氧適能又是另一個面向。營養介入能否提供額外效益，取決於比較條件、實際攝取及訓練背景；不能由單一研究的顯著或不顯著結果，直接決定所有人的飲食。 
阻力訓練與並行訓練 
阻力訓練（RT）以外在阻力安排肌肉工作；本期並行訓練（CT）是在相同的全身阻力課表後，立即增加自行車訓練。 
CT 的總時間及運動暴露較多。試驗比較的是增加騎車的整套安排，沒有隔離等時間、等工作量下的純訓練模式差異。 
source-stated 
指派蛋白質目標與實際攝取 
指派目標是營養諮詢要求達成的攝取量；實際攝取是參與者真正吃進的量。本試驗以自陳飲食紀錄估計後者。 
平均紀錄接近目標，仍不能證明每日精確達標；也不能把自由生活、非等熱量的飲食諮詢，解讀為隔離蛋白質本身的劑量試驗。 
骨骼肌量、瘦體重與肌肥大 
女性試驗的骨骼肌量由 BIA 模型估計；肌酸統合分析的瘦體重包含水分及其他非脂肪組織。肌肥大則涉及肌肉組織大小的增加。 
兩篇的體組成結果並非同一測量，不能直接互換。水分分布、前置條件與儀器誤差都會影響解讀；瘦體重增加不能全部算成新生肌肉。 
cross-source-synthesis 
估計 1-RM 與估計 VO₂max 
女性試驗以負重與完成次數推估最大肌力，並以次最大騎車心率反應推估最大攝氧量。 
沒有直接完成最大重量或量測呼吸氣體。動作熟悉度、騎車經濟性與心率反應可能影響估計結果。 
調整後組間差與組內變化 
調整後組間差比較基線校正後兩條件的第 12 週結果；組內變化則比較同組前後的原始數值。 
CT − RT 為負，不代表 CT 自己下降。女性試驗所有組別原始平均體重都上升，仍可同時出現 CT 的調整後體重低於 RT。 
Hedges’ g、95% CI 與 95% PI 
肌酸研究的 g 是兩組前後變化差異的標準化效果；CI 描述平均效果估計的不確定性，PI 描述未來研究情境可能出現的效果範圍。 
g = 0.55 不是增加 0.55 kg 或改善 55%。平均效果的 CI 不跨零，仍可能伴隨跨零的 PI；兩者回答不同問題。 
未檢出差異與等效 
未檢出差異表示現有設計與資料未提供足夠證據確認差異；等效需要預先界定可接受差異範圍並以合適設計檢驗。 
兩篇都沒有由不顯著結果證明不同營養劑量可互換。女性試驗的檢定力主要針對中至大型交互作用，較小差異仍可能存在。 
肌酸可能增加高強度工作的供能餘裕 
肌酸全文以磷酸肌酸支持快速 ATP 再合成、增加可完成的高強度訓練，以及細胞水合等途徑解釋力量與瘦體重結果。這些是論文討論的機轉背景，統合分析未一致測量完整的中介路徑。 
【cross-source-synthesis】補充後仍需確認是否實際完成更多或更高品質的訓練，以及力量是否改變；不能只用體重增加推定機轉已奏效。 
pmid-42765482 
額外騎車同時改變刺激、時間與恢復需求 
女性試驗的 CT 在重訓後增加騎車，力量測驗較偏向 RT，有氧估計值較偏向 CT。累積疲勞、實際阻力刺激、恢復與測驗特異性都可能參與，但研究沒有直接測量分子或神經肌肉干擾。 
【cross-source-synthesis】力量落後時先查新增騎車與重訓完成量，不把差距自動歸因於蛋白質不足，也不宣稱有氧必然妨礙所有肌肉適應。 
pmid-42735207 
體脂率下降可能來自分母改變 
肌酸統合分析中瘦體重增加、脂肪量未檢出差異，而體脂率略降；作者認為非脂肪部分增加可解釋比例變化。由於水分未被分別統合，無法確定組織與水分各自的貢獻。 
【cross-source-synthesis】同時呈現體重、脂肪量或體脂率、測量條件及力量，不將較低體脂率直接標示為減脂成功。 
83/108 人；流失 23.1% 
女性試驗的實際分析樣本 
40–77 歲女性隨機分派後，83 人完成第 12 週所有結果評估；採完整案例分析，沒有完整意向治療估計。 
−6.68 kg；95% CI −8.32 至 −5.04 
新增騎車條件的腿推估計 1-RM 較低 
第 12 週基線調整後 CT − RT，合併三種蛋白質指派；Holm 調整後 p < 0.001。不是 CT 組自己減少的重量。 
4.53 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹；95% CI 3.80–5.25 
新增騎車條件的有氧估計值較高 
第 12 週調整後 CT − RT；Ekblom–Bak 次最大自行車測驗推估，沒有呼吸氣體量測；Holm 調整後 p < 0.001。 
0.8、1.6、2.2 g·kg⁻¹·日⁻¹ 
試驗指派的蛋白質目標 
以實際體重計算並每週更新，屬自由生活飲食諮詢條件；主要骨骼肌量結果的蛋白質主效應 p = 0.726，不能據此判定等效或最佳攝取量。 
63 項試驗；1,489 人；女性 248 人 
肌酸統合分析的規模與女性代表性 
作者報告男性 970 人、女性 248 人、未報性別 271 人；18–75 歲，各結果使用不同研究子集，人數不可跨結果加總。 
g = 0.55；95% CI 0.38–0.71；95% PI −0.04–1.14 
肌酸的下肢肌力平均加成 
阻力訓練加肌酸相對加安慰劑；排除一個離群效果值後的三層模型。預測區間跨零，不保證每個情境受益。 
單中心、12 週、平行組隨機 2 × 3 因子試驗；依基線骨骼肌量分層，以密封信封隱藏分派，結果評估者盲化。主要推論採基線調整 ANCOVA，分析限 83 位完整案例。 
108 位 40–77 歲女性，每組隨機分派 18 人；過去一年自陳結構化活動少於每週 2 小時，基線蛋白質約低於 0.8 g·kg⁻¹·日⁻¹。完成者各組平均 BMI 多在肥胖範圍。依自陳排除高血壓、第二型糖尿病、心血管疾病等情況；未正式評估停經階段或荷爾蒙治療。 
比較每週 3 次監督全身 RT，與相同 RT 後立即增加騎車的 CT；兩者總時間、工作量及能量消耗未匹配。另指派 0.8、1.6 或 2.2 g·kg⁻¹·日⁻¹蛋白質目標，以飲食諮詢及自陳紀錄支持，沒有控制供餐或等熱量設計。基線與第 12 週量測 BIA 骨骼肌量、體脂率、重複次數推估力量、次最大騎車推估 VO₂max，以及坐站等功能。無不運動對照，無介入後延長追蹤。 
完成與退出 
83/108 人完成；25/108 人退出，流失 23.1%。 
CT 三組完成 14、15、13 人；RT 三組完成 13、14、14 人。退出主要歸因時間限制或失去興趣；退出者基線資料未保留於最終分析資料集。 
Results 3.2；Table 3 
主要結果：BIA 骨骼肌量 
CT − RT：−0.16 kg，95% CI −0.45 至 0.13，p = 0.273；蛋白質主效應 p = 0.726；訓練 × 蛋白質交互作用 p = 0.856。 
第 12 週基線調整結果，n = 83；無法以原始組內增加確認肌肥大，也不能由不顯著證明等效。 
Results 3.3.1；Tables 6、7 
腿推估計最大肌力 
CT − RT：−6.68 kg，95% CI −8.32 至 −5.04；Holm 調整後 p < 0.001。 
第 12 週，合併蛋白質目標的調整後比較；由 2–10 次有效重複的負重測驗估計 1-RM，非直接最大重量。 
Methods 2.4；Results 3.4.1；Table 7 
自行車測驗估計 VO₂max 
CT − RT：4.53 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹，95% CI 3.80–5.25；Holm 調整後 p < 0.001。 
第 12 週基線調整比較；由 Ekblom–Bak 心率反應推估。允许組別不同基線斜率的敏感度模型為 4.62，95% CI 3.98–5.26，相同單位。 
Methods 2.9；Results 3.4.2、3.7；Table 7

A Change Worth Acting On? 
Creatine, confidence after ACL reconstruction, and what a spine screening score can tell us 
Ying and Bing explore when a measurement should change a training decision. They discuss adult creatine trials, physiotherapists' experiences of psychological support after ACL reconstruction, and spine screening in adolescent rhythmic gymnasts, keeping average effects, professional experience, and screening associations distinct.

Interpret standardized strength effects without converting them into personal guarantees. 
Distinguish lean mass, fat mass, and body fat percentage. 
Explain what physiotherapist focus groups can contribute to ACL rehabilitation decisions. 
Distinguish spine screening categories from diagnoses and causal evidence. 
Identify what additional information could support maintaining training, progressing a task, or arranging professional assessment. 
Pronounce edgeSport4Podcast as Edge Sport for Podcast. The digit 4 means for. 
All research content comes from weeklyReport 2026-w40. No relatedIssues evidence is used. 
Creatine source: Resistance training combined with creatine supplementation: a three-level meta-analysis of multidimensional outcomes from strength enhancement to body composition remodeling. https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2718316 
ACL source: From Fear to Function: How Physiotherapists Navigate Psychological Challenges in Patients Undergoing Rehabilitation After ACL Reconstruction. https://doi.org/10.1177/19417381261471381 
Gymnastics source: Risk of Scoliosis in Adolescent Female Rhythmic Gymnasts Compared with Healthy Peers: A Cross-Sectional Study Using the Scoliosis Tele-Screening Test. https://doi.org/10.1177/19417381261485714 
The creatine appendix was unavailable in the supplied evidence. Outcome-specific GRADE details and individual study characteristics require verification. 
The gymnastics paper contains inconsistencies in category percentages, the precise STS-Test P value, and BMI reporting. This script retains reported counts and means. 
The closing decision workflow is an EDGE SPORT operational proposal. The three studies did not validate it as a combined intervention. 
When a number asks for a decision 
The week's central question and the different kinds of evidence available. 
Creatine and the meaning of improvement 
Average strength effects, uncertainty, body composition, and individual relevance. 
Making room for fear in rehabilitation 
What experienced physiotherapists describe and what remains untested. 
A screening result needs interpretation 
Rhythmic gymnastics findings without diagnostic or causal overreach. 
What would change the next step? 
An explicitly unvalidated proposal for documenting decisions and follow-up. 
Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and imagine sitting with your coffee and a training report that looks better than last month's. Before you celebrate or change the plan, what does that improvement actually give you permission to do? 
warm 
I'm Bing, and here on edgeSport4Podcast we're asking when a change is enough to act on. This week's report brings together strength gains, confidence after knee reconstruction, and spine screening, with very different evidence behind each. 
curious 
And the person looking at that report may want a simple answer. Should I keep going, try the next task, or get something checked? Our job today is to see which parts of those questions the research can actually answer. 
reflective 
Let's keep asking what was measured and whose experience it represents. That should make the practical answers more useful. 
clear 
The creatine paper gives us an actual intervention comparison. It pooled randomized trials of adults doing resistance training with creatine against adults doing resistance training with a placebo, so training was part of both sides of the comparison. 
That matters when someone credits everything to the supplement. The authors reported 63 trials and 1,489 adults overall, but different outcomes used different subsets of studies, so we shouldn't add the outcome sample sizes together. 
Before we give the strength result, what does the effect number mean for someone who usually thinks in kilograms? 
They used Hedges' g, which puts the difference in the groups' changes onto a standardized scale. That lets researchers combine different strength measurements, but a value of point five doesn't mean half a kilogram or a fifty percent improvement. 
On that scale, the upper body strength effect was point five four in favor of creatine. For lower body strength, the estimate was point five five after removing one outlying effect value, while the complete analysis gave point six six. 
So the average favors adding creatine, and removing that unusual value made the lower body estimate smaller. How certain is that average? 
For that lower body estimate, the ninety five percent confidence interval ran from point three eight to point seven one. That's uncertainty around the estimated average effect, but a coach also needs to ask how much results might vary across study settings. 
That's where the prediction interval helps. After removing the outlier, it ranged from minus point zero four to one point one four, crossing zero and leaving room for a future study setting with little or no benefit. 
cautious 
And that interval describes possible study effects, rather than giving an individual athlete their own predicted range of strength gains. 
Exactly, and publication bias is another reason to stay measured. A sensitivity analysis that modeled potentially missing effects reduced both strength estimates, although they remained positive. Those modeled effects weren't additional trials that researchers had actually conducted. 
I still find the average strength signal useful for a nutrition discussion. But suppose someone says their scan shows more lean mass and less body fat percentage, so creatine must have built muscle and burned fat. Would you accept both claims? 
I'd separate them. Lean mass increased on average, but lean mass includes water as well as other nonfat tissue, and this analysis couldn't separate those contributions. Calling all of that increase new muscle would go beyond the measurements. 
And a smaller fat percentage can happen when the total changes, even without a clear reduction in the amount of fat? 
Yes, that's the denominator changing. The analysis found a small decrease in body fat percentage but didn't detect a significant difference in fat mass, so it doesn't establish a fat loss benefit from adding creatine to training. 
Then I'd want to know whether the person is getting stronger in a way they value and how they feel about any weight change. Can this paper at least tell us which supplement schedule is most likely to deliver that? 
It didn't identify consistent effects of dose or supplementation schedule on the results. That leaves the best prescription unresolved, and it doesn't establish that all schedules work equally well. The authors rated overall evidence certainty from low to moderate. 
So there's enough to discuss a possible addition, but not enough to promise a particular person's response. 
And that discussion needs context. Women were less represented, diet and hydration reporting were incomplete, and the appendix wasn't available in the supplied evidence. For an individual decision, I'd want their training record, nutrition context, strength changes, and priorities alongside the average result. 
Those priorities become especially visible when someone is rebuilding confidence after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, usually called ACL reconstruction. Our next paper asks how physiotherapists handle psychological challenges during rehabilitation, which is a different question from whether a treatment improves outcomes. 
Different because we're listening to therapists describe their work, rather than following patients through a tested intervention? 
Yes, there were 21 physiotherapists across six focus groups, with 11 from the Netherlands and 10 from Norway. Researchers analyzed the discussions for themes, and there was no intervention comparison or patient follow-up measuring return to sport or reinjury. 
What I found useful was their description of a therapeutic alliance, meaning cooperation built around shared goals, agreed tasks, and trust. They described small achievable goals and gradually approaching feared movements as ways to connect physical progress with confidence. 
Would you call those strategies effective based on these interviews, or would that skip a step in the evidence? 
It would skip the patient's experience and the outcome testing. These are strategies therapists described using, not demonstrated improvements in return rates, though they give us concrete questions about which task feels frightening and whether the athlete feels supported. 
That last question feels easy to miss if the team believes it's already being supportive. The therapists also described group training as potentially helpful, but comparison with someone progressing faster could add pressure, so the same setting may be experienced differently. 
Then a better confidence score wouldn't settle everything. What would you still want to hear from the athlete? 
I'd ask which activity now feels manageable and which still doesn't, as a practical application of the report. The therapists used psychological questionnaires inconsistently, and some relied more on conversation, so this study gives us no universal score that clears someone to progress. 
I'd also ask whose timetable they're trying to meet. The interviews highlighted expectations from coaches, family, and teammates, along with limits in therapists' psychological training and access to referral services. Good intentions don't tell us whether needed support was actually available. 
And we should resist turning every interview example into homework. Some therapists mentioned injury footage or returning to the injury location, but the study didn't establish when those approaches are appropriate or whether they're safe and effective. 
Agreed. I'd use these findings to improve the conversation and clarify support needs, while keeping progression within the person's rehabilitation plan. I'd be more confident about prescribing a particular strategy if research included patient perspectives and measured patient outcomes. 
That wish for information we don't yet have carries into the gymnastics paper. It compared spine screening results in 56 female rhythmic gymnasts and 302 girls of similar age who didn't participate in sport, using a single assessment rather than following changes over time. 
Before the numbers, does a higher score mean more diagnosed scoliosis, or does it identify something that needs interpretation? 
It identifies screening risk. The Scoliosis Tele-Screening Test, or STS-Test, combines information such as family history, maturation, and visible asymmetry, so the total isn't simply a measure of spinal shape. This study didn't confirm scoliosis with imaging. 
With that distinction in place, the gymnasts averaged five point three four points, compared with three point four one in the comparison group. Those are points on the screening tool, and the group averages don't tell us each girl's classification. 
Where did the difference show up when they looked at the categories instead of just the average score? 
Mainly in the middle category. There were 35 gymnasts classified as medium risk out of 56, compared with 60 out of 302 in the comparison group. Keeping those denominators attached matters because the two groups were very different in size. 
And the high risk category didn't show a statistically significant group difference, which doesn't establish that the groups were equal. It also means we shouldn't describe every risk category as elevated or turn the medium risk counts into numbers of diagnosed cases. 
The training hours result is where I can imagine a coach wanting an immediate rule. Within the gymnast group, weekly hours and screening scores had a positive correlation of point four five six, meaning they tended to rise together. 
But we can't turn that association into an hourly ceiling, or assume reducing hours would lower the screening score. 
Right, the study can't establish what came first or separate training from selection and other influences. The girls had at least five years of gymnastics experience and were in competitive tiers three and four, so this isn't a sample of everyone attending a gymnastics class. 
Suppose a parent brings in a medium risk result and asks whether their daughter should stop training. I'd explain that the category needs clinical interpretation and isn't itself a stopping rule. What would help you make the next decision more concrete? 
I'd want the components behind the score, the maturation and training context, and a clinician's assessment of what follow-up is appropriate. The authors suggested screening every six months during growth, but their study didn't test that interval or show that it prevents progression. 
There's also some editorial checking still needed. The paper's percentages don't fully match its category counts, and there are inconsistencies in statistical reporting, so we've retained the reported counts and means without quietly correcting the source. 
That leaves a useful observation with a clear limit. To make stronger prevention decisions, we'd need follow-up connecting these screening results with later clinical outcomes, and evidence testing whether changes in training improve those outcomes. 
So here's our practical proposal from EDGE SPORT, and these studies haven't validated it as a combined process. Before changing training, write down what changed, what the measurement represents, what the athlete wants, and what unanswered question could change the decision. 
encouraging 
I'd add a named person and a date for reviewing the next step. That makes maintaining training, trying an agreed task, or arranging assessment something the team can revisit, without pretending we've discovered a universal progression threshold. 
For this week, discuss creatine through actual strength goals and body changes, ask about specific fears during ACL rehabilitation, and take spine screening concerns to clinical interpretation. Each asks for a different kind of follow-up, and none supplies an automatic personal clearance. 
And leave room for the athlete's answer to change the plan. You'll find the methods, numbers, and remaining uncertainties in the written weekly report and original sources. Thanks for joining us on edgeSport4Podcast, and we'll talk again next week. 
The creatine review reported 63 randomized trials and 1,489 adults, comparing resistance training plus creatine with resistance training plus placebo. 
Outcome analyses use different study subsets with overlapping participants. Their sample sizes must not be added together. This is adult evidence, not an adolescent or ACL-specific supplementation protocol. 
Upper body strength favored creatine with Hedges' g = 0.54, 95% CI 0.37–0.71. Lower body strength was g = 0.66 in the full analysis and g = 0.55 after excluding one outlying effect value. 
Hedges' g expresses standardized between-group differences in change, not kilograms or percentage improvement. Full and outlier-excluded estimates must remain distinguished. 
The outlier-excluded lower body strength estimate had a 95% confidence interval of 0.38–0.71 and a 95% prediction interval of −0.04–1.14. 
The confidence interval concerns uncertainty in the average effect. The prediction interval concerns effects in future study settings and is not an individual prediction interval. Both upper and lower body strength prediction intervals crossed zero. 
Publication-bias sensitivity analyses reduced strength estimates to g = 0.36 for upper body and g = 0.35 for lower body strength, with confidence intervals remaining above zero. 
Trim-and-fill models hypothetical missing effects rather than adding observed trials. This sensitivity analysis used a two-level method treating effects as independent. 
Lean mass increased with g = 0.30, 95% CI 0.18–0.41. Fat mass showed no statistically significant difference, g = −0.10, 95% CI −0.23–0.03, while body fat percentage decreased slightly, g = −0.14, 95% CI −0.26–−0.02. 
Lean mass includes water, and the analysis could not separate water from tissue contributions. A reduced fat percentage does not establish fat loss. Standardized effects are not kilograms or percentage points. 
The review did not identify consistent dose or supplementation-schedule moderation, and the authors rated overall certainty as low to moderate. 
Failure to detect moderation does not establish equivalent regimens or an optimal dose. Women were less represented, contextual reporting was incomplete, and the missing appendix prevents independent verification of detailed outcome-level GRADE assessments. 
The ACL study involved 21 physiotherapists in six focus groups, including 11 from the Netherlands and 10 from Norway. 
Participants were therapists recruited through professional networks, not patients. There was no intervention comparator or longitudinal patient outcome assessment. 
Therapists described trust, shared goals, small milestones, gradual exposure to feared movements, mixed experiences of group training, external pressure, and referral barriers. 
These are professional accounts, not demonstrated improvements in return to sport, reinjury, or patient experience. The study validates no psychological clearance threshold and does not establish injury footage or injury-site visits as safe required tasks. 
The gymnastics study compared 56 female rhythmic gymnasts with 302 similarly aged girls who did not participate in sport. Mean STS-Test scores were 5.34 ± 2.70 versus 3.41 ± 3.39 points. 
This was a single cross-sectional assessment without imaging-confirmed scoliosis. Gymnasts had at least five years of experience and were in tiers 3 and 4. Findings should not be generalized to all gymnastics participants. 
Medium risk counts were 35 of 56 gymnasts and 60 of 302 controls. High risk counts were 2 and 16, respectively, with no statistically significant high risk category difference. 
Counts describe screening categories, not diagnosed cases. A nonsignificant difference does not establish equality. Reported gymnast percentages conflict with counts, so the script uses counts without deriving replacement percentages. 
Weekly training hours correlated with STS-Test scores within the gymnast group, Spearman r = 0.456, P = 0.01. 
The association establishes neither causation nor a safe hourly limit. It does not show that reducing hours lowers scores or prevents disease. 
The gymnastics authors suggested screening every six months during growth. 
The study did not test that interval, longitudinal progression, or the effectiveness of screening-linked interventions. Clinical interpretation is required rather than automatic training cessation based on a category. 
Interpret creatine benefits alongside actual training, strength goals, and body changes. 
Ask about specific feared tasks and perceived support during ACL rehabilitation. 
Treat STS-Test results as screening information requiring interpretation, not diagnoses or automatic stopping rules. 
Record the next step, responsible person, and review date as an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal. 
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for full methods and limitations. 
The speech is synthetic. Ying is locally generated from the supplied female-voice sample, and Bing is locally generated from the supplied male-voice sample. The script is prepared by Codex. This episode is educational and does not provide individualized medical advice or return-to-play clearance.

肌力增加、回場恐懼與脊椎篩檢：哪些訊號足以改變訓練？ 
本週三篇全文分別提供肌酸輔助阻力訓練的效果整合、ACL 重建復健的心理支持經驗，以及青少女韻律體操的脊椎側彎風險篩檢資料。實務上的共同問題是辨認量測代表什麼：瘦體重增加不能全部視為肌肉增生，治療師經驗不能當成療效驗證，篩檢分數也不能取代診斷。 
當肌力、心理準備或脊椎篩檢結果改變時，團隊如何決定維持訓練、分級進階或啟動專業評估？ 
本期包含 3 篇 full-text-open；full-text-web、full-text-local、full-text-excerpt 與 abstract-only 均為 0 篇。已閱讀所附完整文字中的方法、結果、討論、限制、表格、圖說與可見補充說明；肌酸論文提及的 Appendix.docx 未附實際內容，因此不能獨立核對附錄逐篇資料與各結果的 GRADE 細節。三篇分別為隨機試驗統合分析、質性焦點團體研究及橫斷面研究，能支持的效果、經驗與關聯推論須分開處理。 
本週研究地圖 
本封包中，Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition 增加了肌酸與阻力訓練的多結果整合；Sports Health 則分別補上 ACL 復健心理照護的執行經驗與青少女韻律體操的篩檢分布。三者沒有檢驗同一介入，也沒有直接衝突；共同推進的是決策所需的量測解釋與情境辨識。這是本期選文的編輯綜合觀察，不代表整個領域的量化出版趨勢。 
肌酸增加力量與瘦體重的訊號較一致，最佳處方仍未確立 
pmid-42765482 
整合結果支持肌酸作為成人阻力訓練的輔助；脂肪量未檢出顯著差異，劑量及年齡分析不足以建立個人處方。

治療師描述信任關係、小目標及分級暴露的實務角色，但尚未驗證這些策略能提高回場率或降低再傷。

63 項試驗；1,489 人 
肌酸統合分析整體規模 
作者報告的成人總樣本；各結果使用不同研究子集，不可加總各結果人數。 
g = 0.55；95% CI 0.38–0.71 
下肢肌力的組間標準化效果 
阻力訓練加肌酸對照阻力訓練加安慰劑；排除一個離群效果值後，95% 預測區間為 −0.04–1.14。 
21 位治療師；6 場焦點團體 
ACL 心理支持研究的資料來源 
荷蘭 11 位、挪威 10 位；2024 年 3–10 月收集資料，並非 21 位患者的介入追蹤。 
5.34 ± 2.70 對 3.41 ± 3.39 分 
STS-Test 平均分數 
56 位女性韻律體操選手對 302 位未參與運動的同齡女性對照；單次橫斷面篩檢。 
r = 0.456；P = 0.01 
每週訓練時數與 STS-Test 分數的相關 
體操組內的 Spearman 相關；未建立安全訓練時數或降低時數的治療效果。 
決策前必懂的背景 
先區分訓練適應、心理準備與疾病篩檢，再決定下一步。三者都需要追蹤，但適用族群、量測工具與專業處理不同，不能互相充當通關證明。 
瘦體重、脂肪量與體脂率 
瘦體重包含非脂肪組織及水分；脂肪量是脂肪的絕對量，體脂率是脂肪占總體重的比例。 
肌酸使用後體脂率下降可伴隨瘦體重增加，不能直接判定脂肪減少，也不能把全部瘦體重變化視為新生肌肉。 
source-stated 
Hedges' g、信賴區間與預測區間 
本篇 g 表示兩組前後變化差異的標準化效果；信賴區間呈現平均效果估計的不確定性，預測區間呈現未來研究情境可能出現的效果範圍。 
g 不是公斤或改善百分比；肌力平均效果為正，但預測區間跨零，不能保證每個人或每個場域受益。 
心理準備與治療聯盟 
心理準備涉及重返運動的認知判斷、情緒及行為準備；治療聯盟是患者與治療師基於共同目標、任務及信任建立的合作關係。 
量表之外，須了解害怕的具体任務、外界壓力與患者對支持的感受；治療師自認支持充分不代表患者也如此感受。 
回到參與、回到運動、回到表現 
課程將回場區分為受限制的參與、較完整的運動訓練，以及恢復競技表現等不同層次。 
紀錄目前允許的活動與實際完成的層級；一次量表或力量測驗不能代表已完成所有層級。 
inclass-supported 
STS-Test 風險分類與脊椎側彎診斷 
STS-Test 整合病史、成熟狀態及外觀不對稱等項目，用來辨識風險；本研究沒有以影像確診脊椎側彎。 
女性分類為低風險 0–4 分、中風險 5–11 分、高風險 12–15 分。這些是工具分類，並非停訓、手術或確診門檻。 
軀幹旋轉角與全身性關節過度活動 
ATR 是前彎時以脊椎側彎量角器量測的軀幹旋轉角；Beighton 分數評估關節過度活動，本研究採 ≥6/9 分分類。 
ATR 不等同影像 Cobb 角；Beighton 分數也不能單獨判定脊椎側彎或限制運動。 
肌酸可能透過能量供應與訓練容量支持適應 
論文以肌內磷酸肌酸支持快速 ATP 再合成、增加高強度訓練完成能力，以及細胞水合等途徑解釋結果；這些機轉並非本次統合分析直接統一量測的中介效果。 
仍須追蹤實際訓練、飲食與體組成，不能由補充行為直接推定肌肥大。 
可完成的小目標可能協助建立掌握感 
受訪治療師描述，透過可理解的里程碑、個別化溝通與逐步接觸害怕的動作，協助患者連結身體進步與信心。 
將心理反應放入每次訓練討論；目前仍屬治療師經驗，不能宣稱已確認作用機制或療效。

作者討論反覆過伸、非對稱負荷、關節過度活動與成熟因素的可能作用；橫斷面資料無法釐清時間順序，也不能排除選材與其他混雜。

What Would Support the Next Step? 
Fuel, training tradeoffs, and what returning to sport really tells us 
Ying and Bing discuss cycling nutrition guidance, a randomized training and protein trial in middle-aged and older women, and a hip surgery case series. Together they examine what was recommended, what actually happened, and whether the measured outcome answers the athlete's real question. 
en 
host 
Ying 
Evidence guide · female voice 
cohost 
Bing 
Analytical partner · male voice 
pmid-42744290 
pmid-42735207 
pmid-42746137 
Distinguish a nutrition position statement, a randomized trial, and a retrospective case series. 
Interpret assigned nutrition targets separately from actual intake and training exposure. 
Explain why estimated fitness, return to activity, and restored performance answer different questions. 
Identify evidence that could change a training or participation decision without inventing universal thresholds. 
Pronounce edgeSport4Podcast as Edge Sport for Podcast. The digit 4 means for. 
Research claims are based only on weeklyReport 2026-w39 supplied in the private packet. No outside research or relatedIssues claims were added. 
Cycling nutrition: UCI Sports Nutrition Project: Position Statement on Nutrition for Cycling. DOI: 10.1123/ijsnem.2026-0135. Recommendations primarily concern competitive cycling and are not new trial effect estimates. 
Training and protein: Resistance versus concurrent training with three assigned protein targets in middle-aged and older women: a randomized 2 × 3 factorial trial. DOI: 10.1080/15502783.2026.2720742. Complete-case analysis included 83 of 108 randomized participants. 
Hip surgery: Combined Periacetabular Osteotomy and Hip Arthroscopy Results in High Return to Sport Rates in Contact and Noncontact Athletes With Hip Dysplasia. DOI: 10.1177/23259671261466470. Results describe 103 hips in 84 patients. 
The practical recording and reassessment workflow is an EDGE SPORT educational proposal. These studies did not jointly validate it. 
Read the written weekly report and original sources for complete methods, confidence intervals, and limitations. 
The moment before adding more 
Define the next step and recognize the different kinds of evidence. 
Fuel that fits the ride 
Match cycling nutrition recommendations to duration, access, tolerance, and individual response. 
What did adding cycling change? 
Unpack training comparisons, estimated outcomes, attrition, and protein targets. 
Back to activity, back to what? 
Interpret hip-level return rates alongside timing, further procedures, and missing performance data. 
Making the next decision reviewable 
Build an explicitly unvalidated workflow around goals, actual exposure, response, and reassessment. 
Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and I'm thinking about that hopeful moment when someone says they're ready to do more, because this week's question is what would tell us their nutrition, training, and physical response can support that next step? 
warm 
And I'm Bing. Here on edgeSport4Podcast, I'd like to stay with that moment before the calendar fills up, when an extra ride or a return to competition sounds appealing but we haven't quite agreed what success would look like. 
reflective 
That agreement matters because our three sources answer different questions. We've got cycling nutrition guidance built from narrative reviews, a randomized training and protein trial in women, and a retrospective series describing return to activity after combined hip surgery. 
clear 
So before borrowing any number, we need to ask whether it's a recommendation, a comparison, or a description of what happened. 
Exactly, and the cycling statement gives recommendations primarily for elite competitive cycling. It brings together fourteen topic reviews, so it offers a broad planning framework without a newly recruited sample or a single experiment proving the whole package works. 
For a rider planning a longer event, what would you want to know before discussing grams of carbohydrate? 
curious 
I'd want the duration, demands, and chances to eat or drink, along with what their stomach already tolerates. The statement treats terrain, rider roles, and food access as part of the nutrition problem, which makes the plan much more concrete. 
Then the first comparison is event length. For cycling events lasting one to two and a half hours, the statement recommends thirty to sixty grams of carbohydrate per hour, with the actual arrangement shaped by that rider and that event. 
And for events beyond two and a half hours, it gives ninety grams per hour. Those are planning recommendations with context attached, so how would you respond to a rider who wants to jump straight to what professionals reportedly consume? 
I'd ask what benefit they're expecting, because the extra performance benefit of one hundred twenty grams per hour or more remains uncertain. 
cautious 
That's the useful challenge. Above sixty grams per hour, the statement discusses combining carbohydrates such as glucose and fructose that use different intestinal transport pathways, but that explanation still leaves us needing to rehearse the products and check actual tolerance. 
And rehearsal includes whether the food is there when you need it. A target written on a training plan doesn't establish intake, especially when carrying capacity or opportunities to take a bottle constrain what the rider can actually do. 
That gap also brings us to energy availability, meaning the dietary energy left after exercise expenditure, expressed relative to fat free mass. It describes energy available for other bodily functions, while carbohydrate availability asks whether fuel supply matches the particular task. 
So adequate daily energy doesn't automatically tell us that carbohydrate is available around a demanding session. Is that the distinction? 
Yes, timing and task still matter, and a single energy availability estimate can't diagnose relative energy deficiency in sport. The statement also gives a daily protein range of one point six to two point one grams per kilogram of body weight. 
With competitive cyclists as the main context, rather than everyone receiving that range automatically. It also favors responding to menstrual symptoms and individual experience over changing training or diet solely by cycle phase, which keeps the person's response in the conversation. 
That population boundary becomes especially useful with our next paper. It studied women aged forty to seventy seven with little recent structured activity and low reported baseline protein intake, so we're moving into a different training and nutrition setting. 
Different enough that we shouldn't call it a test of the cycling recommendations. What exactly were the women assigned to do? 
They were assigned to supervised resistance training three times weekly or that same prescribed resistance program followed immediately by cycling. Each training condition also had three assigned daily protein targets, making six groups followed over twelve weeks. 
That added cycling is what the paper calls concurrent training, meaning resistance and endurance work in one program. But the extra exercise meant total training time and energy expenditure weren't matched, so this comparison includes the cost of doing more. 
Right, and the prescribed resistance program doesn't prove the completed resistance stimulus was identical. Before the results, there's another constraint worth holding onto, because one hundred eight women were randomized but only eighty three completed the final assessment. 
That's twenty three point one percent attrition. Do the reported comparisons include the women who dropped out? 
They don't, because this was a complete case analysis rather than a full intention to treat analysis. The missing outcomes could affect the comparison, and the report says baseline characteristics couldn't be compared between those who completed and those who withdrew. 
Keeping that in view, the strength comparison favored resistance training alone. At week twelve, the baseline adjusted estimate of maximum leg press strength was six point six eight kilograms lower in the group assigned additional cycling, pooling the protein assignments. 
Lower than the other group, which doesn't mean they lost that much strength. And maximum strength was estimated from repetitions. 
Yes, that's a between group comparison. The cycling group's estimated maximum oxygen uptake was higher by four point five three milliliters per kilogram per minute, after baseline adjustment, so the apparent advantage changes when we change the outcome. 
And oxygen uptake was estimated from heart rate responses during a submaximal cycling test, without directly measuring breathing gases. Since the additional training was also cycling, how much can we say about general fitness or the mechanism behind that difference? 
We can describe the test result, but can't separate added exercise, test familiarity, fatigue, recovery, and physiological adaptation. The study didn't directly measure molecular interference either, so it doesn't establish a biological explanation for the lower estimated leg press result. 
Then a coach needs the person's priority before choosing between those outcomes. Did the trial show a difference in everyday function? 
The thirty second sit to stand test didn't detect a difference between training conditions, and neither did the primary muscle mass estimate. That estimate came from bioelectrical impedance, which is affected by hydration, so we shouldn't turn it into confirmed muscle growth. 
That leaves the protein question, and it's easy to see why people want a simple answer. The assigned daily targets were zero point eight, one point six, and two point two grams per kilogram, supported through dietary counseling during ordinary daily life. 
But counseling isn't controlled feeding. Did they establish actual intake well enough to say those amounts produce equivalent results? 
No, although reported group averages were close to the assigned targets, intake was self reported and diets weren't matched for energy. The main analyses didn't detect overall protein assignment differences, but equivalence wasn't established and some sensitivity findings depended on the model. 
So I wouldn't use this to declare the lowest target sufficient for everyone or the highest necessary. More complete follow up, stronger intake verification, and results in the population I'm advising would change how confidently I'd use it for a nutrition decision. 
That same question about what a result really establishes follows us into the hip paper. This was a single center retrospective series after combined periacetabular osteotomy, a procedure that changes the socket's bony coverage, and hip arthroscopy addressing problems inside the joint. 
And there wasn't a comparison group receiving either procedure alone or nonsurgical care, so we can't use it to rank treatments. The encouraging finding was recorded return to preoperative sport or activity in ninety two of one hundred three hips. 
Hips is the important word there. Those one hundred three hips came from eighty four people, not separate athletes. 
Yes, the reported return proportion was eighty nine point three percent at the hip level. The analysis didn't clearly explain accounting for two hips belonging to the same person, so treating every hip as fully independent would overstate what we know. 
And the recorded return matters to people, but what did returning mean here? The study confirmed sport or activity through records or later recall, without adequately establishing whether people regained their previous competitive level or sustained that performance over years. 
So someone can value being active again while still wanting an answer about competition. We can acknowledge the encouraging participation result and leave the performance question open, rather than making that person feel their remaining goal has already been measured. 
Exactly, and time needs the same care. Among those who returned, the average was two hundred ninety seven point five days, with a standard deviation of one hundred eighty one point three days, describing considerable variation around that average. 
That's a description of this group's experience. It doesn't give the next patient a clearance date or a deadline. 
And that experience includes further treatment, because fifty nine hips had painful fixation hardware removed. Twenty six people who couldn't be contacted were excluded, too, which leaves uncertainty about whether the observed return proportion represents everyone who might otherwise have been included. 
I'd want both of those facts in a discussion of expectations. What about contact sport, because a player might hear that the study found no significant difference and assume their return prospects are the same as in noncontact sport? 
We'd need to slow that inference down. Return was recorded in thirty three of forty contact sport hips and fifty nine of sixty three noncontact sport hips, and the nonsignificant comparison doesn't establish equivalence or rule out an important difference. 
For a stronger treatment discussion, I'd want direct comparisons and longer tracking of competitive performance. For an individual's next activity step, this series leaves us needing the surgical and rehabilitation team's assessment, because it supplies no validated clearance test or universal progression schedule. 
That brings me back to the hopeful person asking to do more. Our EDGE SPORT proposal is to write down the goal, actual training and intake, symptoms and functional response, and the next review, while recognizing that this workflow hasn't been validated by these studies. 
encouraging 
I like having something we can revisit. What would actually change the plan when that next review comes around? 
Under that proposal, we'd reconsider if food access or gut symptoms prevented planned fueling, or if extra cycling undermined the chosen strength goal. We'd check the actual exposure and measurement conditions before interpreting the change, with postoperative activity decisions staying with the treating team. 
And we should let the person help choose what matters, because more cycling, a higher intake target, and a return record each leave something unanswered. I'd want us to agree beforehand which result would justify continuing and which would make us reconsider. 
Then our practical recap is to fit fuel to the ride, count the added training, and keep return to activity separate from restored performance. Undetected differences don't establish equivalence, and our recording proposal gives the next conversation a starting point without supplying a universal threshold. 
That's a useful place to leave the coffee and open the notebook. You'll find the full comparisons and limitations in the written weekly report and original sources, and we hope your next discussion starts with what you're trying to achieve and what would support it. 
The cycling statement integrates 14 narrative topic reviews and primarily addresses elite competitive cycling. 
It has no newly recruited intervention sample or unified effect estimate. Recommendation certainty varies by topic. 
Recommended carbohydrate intake during cycling events is 30–60 g/hour for events lasting 1–2.5 hours and 90 g/hour for events longer than 2.5 hours. 
These are context-dependent recommendations requiring attention to access and gastrointestinal tolerance. Additional benefit from 120 g/hour or more remains uncertain. 
The cycling statement recommends daily protein intake of 1.6–2.1 g/kg body weight. 
This is guidance primarily for competitive cyclists, not a new dose-response trial or a universal prescription for all populations. 
Energy availability expresses dietary energy remaining after exercise expenditure relative to fat-free mass. 
One estimate cannot diagnose relative energy deficiency in sport. Adequate total energy does not establish appropriate carbohydrate availability for a specific session. 
The cycling statement does not support universally changing training or diet solely according to menstrual cycle phase. 
Individual symptoms and responses remain relevant. This is not evidence that symptoms should be ignored. 
The 12-week randomized trial assigned 108 women aged 40–77 to two training conditions and three protein targets. Eighty-three completed assessment, with 25 withdrawals representing 23.1% attrition. 
Analysis used complete cases rather than full intention to treat. Menopausal status and hormone therapy were not formally assessed. 
Concurrent training added cycling immediately after the prescribed resistance program, performed three times weekly. 
Training time and energy expenditure were not matched. Incomplete reporting of completed training prevents confirmation of equal achieved resistance stimuli. 
At week 12, the baseline-adjusted concurrent-training minus resistance-training difference in estimated leg press one-repetition maximum was −6.68 kg, with 95% CI −8.32 to −5.04. 
This pooled comparison across protein assignments is not a within-group strength loss. Strength was estimated from repetitions, and the result does not establish a molecular interference mechanism. 
The adjusted concurrent-training minus resistance-training difference in estimated VO₂max was 4.53 mL/kg/min, with 95% CI 3.80–5.25. 
VO₂max was estimated with the submaximal Ekblom–Bak cycling test, not directly measured using respiratory gases. Confidence intervals were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. 
Training-condition differences were not detected for estimated skeletal muscle mass or 30-second sit-to-stand performance. 
Adjusted differences were −0.16 kg for BIA skeletal muscle mass, 95% CI −0.45 to 0.13, and 0.27 repetitions for sit-to-stand, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.67. Nondetection does not establish equivalence, and BIA does not confirm hypertrophy. 
Assigned protein targets were 0.8, 1.6, and 2.2 g/kg/day. Main analyses did not detect overall protein-assignment differences. 
Intake was self-reported under dietary counseling, without controlled feeding or matched energy intake. Some sensitivity findings depended on the model, and complete supplementary tables were unavailable in the packet. Neither equivalence nor a universal minimum requirement was established. 
The hip series recorded return to preoperative sport or activity in 92 of 103 hips, or 89.3%, from 84 patients. 
The denominator is hips, not independent athletes. This single-center retrospective series lacked a direct treatment comparator and did not clearly describe adjustment for correlation between two hips from one patient. 
Match cycling fuel to the task, food access, and tolerance. 
Count additional cycling as added exposure and judge outcomes against the person's goal. 
Undetected protein differences do not establish equivalent doses or universal sufficiency. 
Read hip return rates with their hip-level denominator, further procedures, and unknown competitive outcomes. 
Record the goal, actual exposure, response, and reassessment plan as an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal. 
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for full methods and limitations. 
The speech is synthetic. Ying is locally generated from the supplied female-voice sample, and Bing is locally generated from the supplied male-voice sample. The script is prepared by Codex. This episode is educational and does not provide individualized medical advice or return-to-play clearance.

增加負荷之前：營養、訓練與回場能力如何對齊？ 
本週三篇全文共同提醒：營養、訓練與回場決策，必須先界定目標、實際暴露與測量方式。自行車營養立場聲明提供依任務補給的框架；中高齡女性試驗顯示不同訓練組合的結果取捨，但未建立蛋白質劑量等效；髖部聯合手術病例系列則呈現較高回場比例，仍不能代表恢復原有競技表現。 
當準備增加訓練或運動參與時，團隊如何確認營養支持、實際負荷與功能反應足以支撐下一步？

能量可用性（EA） 
飲食能量扣除運動能量消耗後，以去脂體重標準化，表示可供其他生理功能使用的能量。 
計算形式為（能量攝取 − 運動能量消耗）/去脂體重；自行車聲明提出約 40–45 kcal·kg 去脂體重⁻¹·日⁻¹的日常目標，不能當作單次測量即可診斷 REDs 的界線。

指派蛋白質目標與實際攝取 
指派目標是飲食諮詢希望達成的量；實際攝取是參與者真正吃進的量。 
女性試驗依自陳紀錄估計攝取，未以控制供餐或客觀標記確認；應解讀為飲食諮詢條件的比較。 
並行訓練（CT） 
同一訓練計畫結合阻力與耐力訓練；本試驗是在阻力訓練後立即增加騎車。 
評估新增有氧時須把額外時間與恢復需求一起計入，不能把本研究當作等總量的訓練模式比較。 
估計值與直接測量 
估計值以儀器模型或公式推算目標能力，不等同直接測得組織大小或最大攝氧量。 
BIA 骨骼肌量、重複次數推估 1-RM、Ekblom–Bak 推估 VO₂max，應保留各自的水分、技術與測驗熟悉度限制。 
回到參與、回到運動、回到表現 
三者分別追蹤重新參與活動、恢復目標運動，以及恢復原有或目標競技能力；所附回場課程與第 37 週週報支持將回場視為連續過程。 
髖部研究主要確認是否返回術前運動或活動，沒有充分量化競技層級與表現；實務紀錄應將三個層次分欄。

未檢出差異表示現有資料未提供足夠統計證據；等效則需要能支持差異落在預定可接受範圍內的設計與分析。

燃料供應與腸胃耐受共同限制補給 
自行車聲明指出，碳水可提供外源燃料、支持肝醣利用及中樞感受；較高攝取量可透過葡萄糖與果糖的不同腸道運輸途徑提高供應，但仍受個人耐受與賽事後勤限制。 
補給量、產品組成與取得時機需要一起演練；不能只提高標示的每小時克數。 
額外騎車與測驗特異性可能共同影響結果 
女性試驗中 CT 增加了騎車暴露，且有氧結果也由騎車測驗推估；疲勞、恢復與熟悉度可能參與組間差異，但研究未直接量測分子干擾或心血管適應。 
將力量與有氧結果分開追蹤，避免以單一改善推論所有功能均改善。 
結構矯正不能單獨代表運動能力 
PAO 與關節鏡分別處理髖部骨性覆蓋及關節內相關問題；本病例系列未找到影像參數或 mHHS 與回場的顯著關聯，不能據此確認結構、症狀與競技能力之間的因果路徑。 
術後追蹤需另問實際運動參與與表現，影像及日常功能量表不宜獨自承擔回場判斷。

自行車補給要配合任務；高攝取量仍須通過耐受與效益檢驗 
聲明把自行車營養從每日總量延伸到賽程、角色、車上補給機會與食物後勤。其核心是支持關鍵課程與長期健康，並將體重視為需要解讀的指標；超高碳水、低碳水訓練、補充品及新科技的應用，仍各有未解問題。 
同一運動內的賽程與角色差異很大，沒有適用全部自行車項目的單一最佳營養模式。 
超過 60 g/小時的碳水目標需考慮多重可運輸碳水與腸胃演練；觀察到職業選手吃得更多，不等於已證明額外表現效益。 
能量與碳水不足均可能影響健康；體態管理應採季節性彈性範圍，避免長期追逐最低體重。 
目前不支持只依月經週期階段普遍調整訓練或飲食，宜依症狀與個人反應調整。 
功率計可協助估計需求；健康運動員的連續血糖監測仍有延遲、準確度及決策用途限制。 
支持課程對低能量可用性與健康的重視，並將第 36 週的補水及腸胃演練延伸到自行車賽程與每日補給。另一方面，聲明不支持僅依週期分期安排強弱課表，對所附女性課程的概括分期建議構成修正；這不等於否認個別症狀，也不是對 ACL 風險的直接檢驗。

A Slower Fastball, a Better Question 
How to notice meaningful changes without turning a measurement into a diagnosis 
Ying and Bing explore four studies on pitching, walking, lumbar and hamstring diagnoses, and gut microbes and fatigue. They distinguish useful assessment clues from personal prediction, then discuss an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT workflow for responding to persistent performance changes. 
en 
host 
Ying 
Evidence guide · female voice 
cohost 
Bing 
Analytical partner · male voice 
pmid-42704785 
pmid-42711120 
pmid-42714926 
pmid-42719368 
Distinguish group associations from individual diagnosis and prediction. 
Explain pitch-specific trends, within-game variability, and between-group slope differences. 
Interpret walking volume and PK30 without converting observational findings into prescriptions. 
Recognize the limits of diagnostic coexistence and predominantly animal-based fatigue research. 
Separate research findings from the proposed EDGE SPORT monitoring workflow. 
All research claims derive from the supplied 2026-w38 weekly report. The proposed monitoring workflow has not been validated as an injury-prevention intervention. 
Pitching: 27 MLB surgical cases and 54 matched controls; the final-five-appearance analysis included 22 eligible cases. https://doi.org/10.1177/23259671261431839 
Walking: the all-cause and cardiovascular mortality analyses use different denominators. PK30 averages the highest 30 minute-level cadences, which need not be consecutive. https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2025-111173 
Lumbar and hamstring diagnoses: retrospective medical-record associations do not establish symptom origin or support routine imaging. https://doi.org/10.1097/JSM.0000000000001487 
Natural products and fatigue: 25 animal studies and one human study; no pooled effect estimate. https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2728356 
Consult the written EDGE SPORT 2026-w38 report for the complete evidence tables, uncertainty statements, proposed workflow, and original-source links. 
When a familiar number changes 
The central question: when should a performance trend prompt assessment? 
What the pitching study actually measured 
Small athlete samples, pitch-specific trends, and the limits of group differences. 
Walking: quantity and intensity 
Defining PK30 and interpreting mortality associations with their reference group. 
Keeping symptom explanations open 
Lumbar and hamstring diagnoses coexist more often, without establishing causation. 
Gut mechanisms and human evidence 
Why a largely animal-based review cannot establish an athlete supplement plan. 
A practical response with visible uncertainty 
An unvalidated proposal for checking data, assessing symptoms, adjusting exposure, and reviewing the response. 
Imagine you're watching a pitcher you know well. The fastball looks a little slower again, and afterward they say, 'I'm just not bouncing back the way I usually do.' That leaves a very human question: do we change something now, or are we reading too much into a number? I'm Ying, and this is edgeSport4Podcast. 
warm 
And I'm Bing. I'd want to take that person seriously without making the graph sound like a diagnosis. This week's central question is how a team checks a persistent velocity decline, considers changes to pitching exposure, and starts an assessment. What evidence would actually change the next decision? 
curious 
We've got four sources: MLB pitching data, walking and mortality, lumbar and hamstring diagnoses, and a review of natural products, gut microbes, and fatigue. They don't test one shared intervention. Together, they give us different chances to practice the same editorial discipline: say what was measured, then keep the conclusion inside that boundary. 
clear 
And let's keep two conversations visible. One is what the studies found. The other is what EDGE SPORT proposes a team could do with that information. A sensible workflow can still be untested. I'd hate for listeners to hear our practical suggestions and assume researchers have already shown that following them prevents shoulder surgery. 
cautious 
The pitching study looked backward at 27 MLB pitchers who underwent their first shoulder capsulolabral repair, involving the shoulder capsule and labrum, and 54 matched controls. Matching included season, pitching role, throwing side, age, and pitch count. These were selected surgical cases, so this isn't a study of every possible reason a pitcher's shoulder might hurt. 
The tracking dataset sounds enormous: 161,979 pitches across 3,347 appearances. But those pitches came from a small number of people. Repeated observations help describe each player's pattern; they don't turn the study into one with 161,979 independent athletes. Ying, what stood out when the researchers compared the groups over time? 
There were two different layers. In the previous season, the eventual surgical cases had higher average velocity for some fastballs and higher standardized spin overall. The more consistent velocity declines appeared later in the injury season and before injured-list placement. So a higher-output background and a recent downward trend are separate observations. 
Let's slow down for the number that could easily become a dashboard alarm. In the final five appearances, the primary-fastball slope difference was minus 0.195 miles per hour per appearance, with a 95 percent confidence interval from minus 0.301 to minus 0.090. That analysis included 22 eligible cases and matched controls. What exactly is that difference comparing? 
reflective 
It's the cases' rate of change minus the controls' rate of change. It isn't a claim that every injured pitcher lost exactly that much velocity each outing. And it isn't a personal removal threshold. The primary breaking ball also showed a more negative slope in cases, but neither result came with a validated individual prediction rule. 
There's also a timing problem. Injured-list placement gives the researchers a date, but it doesn't tell them when symptoms or tissue changes began. The decline could reflect a developing problem, fatigue, or other influences they couldn't separate. So calling this an early warning requires care: early relative to the list entry isn't necessarily early relative to the injury. 
Another finding made me pause: cases had lower within-game variability in velocity and arm angle in pooled analyses. Here, variability means the standard deviation of individual pitches of the same type within a game. Bing, if a coach hears that consistent pitching was associated with surgical cases, should they encourage a less repeatable delivery? 
No. That would turn an association into a treatment. The authors explicitly don't recommend deliberately increasing movement variability or reducing competitive output because of this finding. Statcast didn't measure tissue stress or muscle activation. Also, lower variation in arm angle doesn't mean a lower average arm angle. Those are different quantities, with different interpretations. 
That's helpful. A player could have very similar velocities within each outing while their average velocity falls across outings. Consistency within a game and change between games can coexist. For a team, the useful question becomes whether comparable pitches show a persistent change, alongside what the pitcher reports about symptoms and recovery. 
And I'd need prospective evidence before trusting an automatic alert: how often does it correctly identify a problem, how often does it miss one, and does acting on it improve outcomes? This study doesn't answer those questions. No decline can't clear a shoulder, either. The direct evidence is from MLB, with uncertain transfer to youth, amateur, or postoperative pitchers. 
Let's leave the mound for a walk. The next study asks about the combination of how much people step and how briskly they step. Its all-cause mortality analysis included 64,743 UK Biobank adults, averaging 61.5 years old, with 1,697 deaths over a median eight years. It followed observed activity; it didn't assign walking plans. 
Activity came from seven days of wrist-worn monitoring. Daily steps describe accumulated stepping volume. The intensity measure, PK30, averages the day's 30 highest minute-level step rates, then averages across valid days. Those minutes don't have to be consecutive. So, Ying, someone taking a continuous half-hour walk isn't automatically doing the exact exposure measured here. 
Right. And an ordinary average cadence on a watch isn't automatically PK30. The comparison group matters just as much: fewer than 5,000 daily steps, with PK30 at the overall fifth percentile, about 45 steps a minute. Every hazard ratio we're about to mention is relative to that joint reference, rather than a comparison with everyone else. 
With fewer than 5,000 steps and PK30 of 80, the all-cause mortality hazard ratio was 0.72, with a 95 percent interval of 0.54 to 0.97. At 5,000 to 7,500 steps and PK30 of 60, it was 0.70, interval 0.58 to 0.86. Different combinations showed lower hazards. Can we call those two routes equally effective? 
We can't. They weren't directly tested for equivalence, and nobody was randomized to either route. Another combination, 7,500 to 10,000 steps with PK30 around 100, had a hazard ratio of 0.57, interval 0.47 to 0.69. That's a relative hazard association during follow-up, not an individual's probability of dying or a guaranteed benefit from changing their routine. 
The uncertainty isn't uniform, either. Under 5,000 steps with PK30 of 90 had an estimate of 0.64, but the interval ran from 0.32 to 1.32, crossing one. And an apparent upturn at the high end didn't persist across modeling approaches. We shouldn't turn that curve into a claim that more or faster walking causes harm. 
What would you take into a conversation with someone who finds step targets discouraging? I'd want to understand whether the obstacle is time, preference, or walking ability. These results make room to discuss volume and intensity together. But they don't provide a personal starting speed, a safe progression rate, or evidence that one watch's numbers match the research algorithm. 
I'd use that opening, while remembering the measurement was one week representing years of follow-up. Unmeasured differences and undiagnosed illness could still influence the association. Steps also miss activities such as swimming and cycling. The practical gain is a more flexible conversation about activity, with the person's circumstances in view, rather than a newly mandatory number. 
Our third study shifts from activity measurements to medical records. Researchers compared 1,269 people with a hamstring diagnosis with 1,269 demographically matched controls in one healthcare system. Ages ranged from 15 to 94. This was a general healthcare sample, which matters if we're tempted to tell a competitive sprinter that the percentages describe their situation. 
Lumbar pathology appeared in 469 records in the hamstring group and 318 controls: reported as 37 percent and 25.1 percent. These were existing diagnostic or imaging records, including conditions such as disc degeneration or herniation. The study didn't establish which came first. Ying, is the takeaway simply to look at the back whenever a hamstring hurts? 
I'd phrase it more selectively. When posterior thigh symptoms recur or the local explanation doesn't fit, a clinician can consider lumbar history and assessment. Coexisting records don't establish where pain comes from. The study also didn't confirm every hamstring diagnosis with one uniform procedure, so we can't assume every record represented the same kind of structural injury. 
The adjusted odds ratio was 1.84, accounting for age and body mass index, and the source didn't provide a confidence interval. Odds aren't the same as probability, so '84 percent more likely to develop lumbar disease' would be wrong. These are coexistence data, without a demonstrated sequence leading from one diagnosis to another. 
There's a detection issue too: people with hamstring symptoms might receive more lumbar investigations, making lumbar findings easier to discover. Some controls could have received care elsewhere. Bing, what would change your decision about further assessment here? I don't want the sensible idea of considering another symptom source to quietly become routine imaging for everyone. 
I'd leave the imaging decision with the clinician's individual history and examination. The study didn't test whether routine imaging improves outcomes. It gives a reason to keep an explanation open, especially when the local picture is incomplete. It doesn't prove a lumbar cause, and it doesn't establish a preventive lumbar treatment for people with hamstring diagnoses. 
That brings us to fatigue, where a compelling explanation can feel especially welcome. The natural-products review included 26 studies: 25 in mice or rats and one in humans. The animal work mainly used exercise-to-exhaustion models. Because the studies differed substantially, the authors didn't pool them into a single effect estimate. 
The proposed connection is interesting: products might alter gut microbes and their metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids, with possible links to energy regulation, the gut barrier, and inflammation. But seeing microbes and fatigue measures change together doesn't prove that the microbial change produced the performance effect. Did any studies get closer to testing that connection? 
Some animal experiments used antibiotics or fecal microbiota transfer to probe microbial involvement. That adds mechanistic support in those models. It doesn't establish the whole pathway in every study or show that an athlete will benefit. Even the directions of microbial changes weren't consistent enough to define one universal microbiome target. 
The human study involved matcha alongside resistance training in healthy, untrained young men. The review described lower subjective fatigue in week one, without an effect size or confidence interval. The eight-week leg-strength finding was described as a trend. That sounds like a reason for better human trials. What stops us from making even a modest product recommendation? 
The thin human evidence, unclear sample-group reporting, and limited transfer to trained athletes all matter. We shouldn't reconstruct a total sample from ambiguous table entries or promote a strength trend into a clear benefit. This review can't rank products reliably, establish an athlete dosing plan, or tell us that a pitcher's persistent fatigue originates in the gut. 
I'd change my confidence with clearer controlled human studies in relevant populations, reporting meaningful effects and uncertainty. For now, the mechanism remains a research question. A nutrition discussion can include any new products someone is using, but microbiome testing or a supplement shouldn't replace assessment of unexplained fatigue and declining performance on the strength of this review. 
Let's return to our pitcher. From here, we're describing the EDGE SPORT workflow proposal in the weekly report, not an intervention the studies validated. First, check whether the signal is comparable: same pitch type, consistent units and measurement process, and a similar role or task. Keep training and game contexts identifiable, and mark missing data. 
I'd put the athlete's account beside that data immediately: symptoms, perceived recovery, pitch counts, and recent training. But I want to challenge the order slightly. If symptoms or worsening function make continued pitching questionable, data cleaning shouldn't delay professional assessment. Under the proposal, stop that session and involve the athletic training or medical team; existing medical restrictions take priority. 
Agreed. The spreadsheet doesn't get first refusal on care. If the team considers continued activity appropriate within limits, it can document an exposure adjustment and its reason. That might involve volume, intensity, density, or role. The report supplies no validated reduction percentage, rest duration, or velocity cutoff, so we shouldn't create one to make the plan look more complete. 
Then make the next review concrete: who records the response, what changed, and what the team will reconsider before adding demands. The report proposes checking symptoms and recovery after activity and the next day. That timing is an operational suggestion. A single rebound in velocity doesn't establish recovery, and keeping good records doesn't prove the process prevents injury. 
So my practical recap is: compare like with like, listen to the athlete, and use persistent change to open assessment. Keep alternative explanations available without assigning a diagnosis. Walking combinations can broaden an activity conversation; lumbar records can broaden a clinical question; gut mechanisms can guide research. None supplies a shortcut to an individual pitching decision. 
encouraging 
And ask what would change the next decision, then record the answer and revisit it. You can find the full numbers, limitations, and original sources in the written EDGE SPORT report. The pitching study included 27 MLB pitchers undergoing first capsulolabral repair and 54 matched controls, with 161,979 pitches across 3,347 appearances. 
Retrospective matched case-control data. Pitches are repeated observations from a small athlete sample, not independent participants; subgroup sample sizes differ. 
In the last-five-appearance analysis with 22 eligible cases and matched controls, the primary-fastball slope difference was −0.195 mph per appearance, 95% CI −0.301 to −0.090. 
Case-minus-control slope difference, not each case's absolute decline or an individual diagnostic cutoff. Injured-list placement does not establish symptom onset. No validated prediction accuracy or intervention benefit was reported. 
Cases showed lower within-game velocity and arm-angle variability in pooled analyses. 
Variability refers to within-game, same-pitch-type standard deviations. Lower arm-angle variability does not mean lower mean arm angle. The findings do not justify deliberately increasing movement variability. 
The walking all-cause mortality analysis included 64,743 adults, mean age 61.5 years, and 1,697 deaths over median follow-up of 8.0 years. 
Prospective observational UK Biobank analysis using seven-day baseline wrist monitoring. The separate cardiovascular analysis used 70,075 participants and must not share the all-cause denominator. 
PK30 averages the day's highest 30 minute-level cadences, which need not be consecutive, then averages across valid monitoring days. 
Not continuous brisk walking for 30 minutes, ordinary average cadence, or running-technique cadence. Direct comparison requires compatible measurement definitions. 
Against fewer than 5,000 steps/day and PK30 at the overall fifth percentile, approximately 45 steps/minute, fewer than 5,000 steps with PK30 80 had HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54–0.97); 5,000–7,500 steps with PK30 60 had HR 0.70 (0.58–0.86). 
All-cause mortality associations against a shared reference, not randomized intervention effects or a direct equivalence test between the combinations. 
At 7,500–10,000 steps/day and PK30 approximately 100 steps/minute, the all-cause mortality HR was 0.57 (95% CI 0.47–0.69). 
Relative hazard against the specified joint reference; not an individual absolute risk, guaranteed benefit, or optimal personal prescription. 
Below 5,000 steps/day with PK30 90, the all-cause mortality HR was 0.64 (95% CI 0.32–1.32); high-end curve upturns were not consistent across models. 
The interval crosses one. Neither this estimate nor model-sensitive curve shapes establishes that more or faster walking causes harm. 
Each lumbar/hamstring comparison group contained 1,269 people, aged 15–94. Lumbar pathology records occurred in 469 hamstring-group participants and 318 controls, reported as 37% versus 25.1%. 
General healthcare records, not an athlete-specific cohort or prospective incidence estimate. Temporal order, uniform diagnostic confirmation, and causal symptom origin were not established. 
The age- and BMI-adjusted odds ratio linking hamstring diagnosis with lumbar pathology was 1.84; the source did not provide a confidence interval. 
An odds ratio cannot be restated as an 84% increase in disease probability. Detection bias and incomplete records remain possible; routine imaging benefit was not tested. 
The natural-products review included 26 studies: 25 animal studies and one human study; heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis. 
Predominantly animal exhaustion models provide limited direct evidence for trained athletes. Some mechanistic experiments probed microbial involvement, but this does not establish clinical efficacy. 
The human matcha study involved healthy untrained young men undertaking resistance training; lower subjective fatigue was described at week one without an effect size or confidence interval, and the eight-week leg-strength result was described as a trend. 
Ambiguous sample-group reporting does not support reconstructing a total sample. The findings do not establish a supplement prescription, product ranking, or clear strength benefit. 
Check comparable pitch-specific data alongside symptoms, exposure, and recovery. 
Use persistent changes to prompt assessment; no study supplies an individual injury or clearance threshold. 
Interpret walking volume and intensity together without promising causal benefits. 
Keep alternative symptom sources open without assuming lumbar causation or ordering routine imaging. 
Require stronger human evidence before converting gut mechanisms into supplement recommendations. 
Document adjustments and reassessment; the EDGE SPORT workflow remains unvalidated.

球速下降時：如何從監測訊號走向負荷調整？ 
本週四篇研究共同提醒：量測到的表現、活動量與病理關聯，需要放回族群、時間趨勢及研究設計中解讀。步數與步行強度提供不同的健康活動路徑；腰椎與腿後肌診斷的共存、投手傷前球速下降，則支持更完整的評估與追蹤。天然產物調節腸道菌相的抗疲勞研究仍以動物為主，本週實務方案因此聚焦於投手表現下降後的監測、負荷調整與臨床討論。 
當投手球速持續下降或恢復不如預期時，團隊如何核對資料、調整暴露並啟動評估，而不把群體關聯當成個人傷害診斷？ 
本期納入四篇來源：full-text-web 三篇、full-text-open 一篇；full-text-local、full-text-excerpt 與 abstract-only 均為零。已閱讀提供的完整嵌入文字，包括方法、結果、討論、限制、可取得的表格、圖說與附錄；步行研究的部分表格與線上補充材料僅有標題或正文轉述，因此只採用實際提供的數值。全文可讀不等於因果證據充分：本期包含一篇以動物研究為主的描述性系統綜述、一篇前瞻性觀察世代研究及兩篇回溯性比較研究，均未驗證本報提出的監測流程能降低傷害。 
本週研究地圖 
本期選文橫跨 JISSN 的腸道菌相與疲勞、BJSM 的步數與死亡率、Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine 的腰椎與腿後肌診斷，以及 OJSM 的投球追蹤與肩部手術。共同進展是把單一指標放進多維情境：活動量搭配強度、局部症狀搭配其他可能來源、平均表現搭配個人時間趨勢。四篇並未測試相同介入或結果，不能合併成統一效應；最明顯的證據落差是天然產物機轉研究豐富，但人體應用資料稀少。 
量與強度的共同判讀 
pmid-42711120 
pmid-42719368 
步行研究顯示步數與 PK30 的組合具有不同死亡率關聯；投球研究顯示高輸出背景與後續球速下降是不同層次的訊號。兩者支持多維判讀，但健康步行與職業投球不能互換處方。 
mixed 
表現下降與症狀來源需要重新評估 
pmid-42714926 
腿後肌診斷者較常有腰椎病理紀錄；需要肩關節囊盂唇修補的投手，在傷兵名單登錄前出現較明顯球速下降。兩者提供評估線索，尚未建立診斷或預測門檻。

26 篇：25 篇動物、1 篇人體 
天然產物綜述的研究組成 
檢索截至 2026 年 3 月；因研究異質性大，未進行統合分析。 
64,743 人；1,697 件全因死亡 
步行研究的全因死亡分析規模 
UK Biobank，中位追蹤 8.0 年，平均年齡 61.5 歲。 
HR 0.57；95% CI 0.47–0.69 
步數與 PK30 組合的全因死亡關聯 
每日 7,500–10,000 步、PK30 約 100 步／分鐘；共同參照為每日少於 5,000 步且 PK30 位於整體第 5 百分位。 
469/1,269 與 318/1,269 
有腰椎病理紀錄的人數 
腿後肌診斷組與人口特徵配對對照組，分別為來源報告的 37% 與 25.1%。 
−0.195 mph／出賽；95% CI −0.301 至 −0.090 
主要速球球速的組間斜率差 
傷兵名單登錄前最後五次出賽；22 名符合條件的手術病例及配對對照，屬病例減對照的時間趨勢差。 
決策前必懂的背景 
本週需區分「量測的是什麼」、「關聯發生在哪個族群」及「是否已驗證可據此採取行動」。實務核心是建立可比較的個人資料，再把變化連回症狀、活動暴露與專業評估；機轉假說與群體統計不能直接成為補充品、停訓或回場處方。 
每日步數與 PK30 
每日步數描述步行與跑步的累積量；PK30 是一天中步頻最高、但不必連續的三十分鐘之平均步頻，再跨有效監測日平均。 
PK30 不是連續快走三十分鐘，也不是跑步技術步頻。只有能取得相同定義的逐分鐘資料，才能直接對照研究暴露。 
source-stated 
場內變異與跨場趨勢 
投球研究的場內變異是同場、同球種逐球數值的標準差；跨場趨勢則是不同出賽之間平均值如何改變。 
不能把場內球速較一致與跨場球速下降混成同一訊號，也不能因病例變異較低，就要求投手刻意增加動作變異。 
組間斜率差 
最後五場投球模型的效應是病例組相對對照組，每次出賽變化速度的差異。 
−0.195 mph／出賽不是所有病例的固定下降速度，也不是個人換投界線。 
診斷共存與病因 
腰椎研究比較病歷中的腿後肌診斷與腰椎病理是否同時存在，沒有確立兩者發生先後或因果方向。 
腿後肌疼痛可促使臨床人員考慮腰椎來源，但病歷共存不能證明疼痛來自腰椎，也不支持所有人常規接受影像檢查。 
腸道菌相變化與菌相介導 
菌相變化是介入後微生物組成改變；菌相介導則需要更直接的實驗證據支持菌相參與效果產生。綜述中部分動物研究使用抗生素或糞菌移植檢驗此問題。 
菌群與疲勞指標相關，尚不足以選定人體補充品或設定菌相檢測目標。 
回到參與、回到運動、回到表現 
所附前期週報將回場分為恢復部分參與、恢復運動活動及恢復原有表現三個層次；本報沿用此概念安排討論。 
完成調整後的投球活動，不等於已能承受完整比賽，也不代表恢復原有競技表現；本週研究未提供肩部術後各階段的通關門檻。 
cross-source-synthesis 
腸道代謝物與能量調節 
天然產物綜述提出，短鏈脂肪酸可能透過 AMPK／PGC-1α 相關訊號、腸道屏障及發炎調節，連結菌相與骨骼肌功能；主要依據來自動物模型，並非每篇都直接測量完整路徑。 
這是後續人體研究的候選機轉，不能據此把持續球速下降歸因於腸道菌相。 
腰椎病理可能影響後側大腿症狀 
腰椎研究討論神經根相關轉移痛與神經性肌力下降的可能性，但本研究未以神經診斷測試確認這條因果鏈。 
當局部診斷無法充分解釋症狀時，可由臨床人員擴大評估範圍。 
高輸出、重複負荷與球速下降 
投球研究提出，高輸出與高度重複的動作可能集中累積組織負荷，而發展中的疼痛、不穩定或神經肌肉抑制可能限制球速。這些是討論中的解釋，Statcast 未直接測量組織應力或肌肉活化。 
保留球種別球速趨勢的監測價值，同時透過症狀詢問與臨床評估檢查可能原因。 
monitoring 
assessment 
training 
sport-medicine 
performance 
從單一數字走向有情境的監測 
本期研究提供的進展，是讓數據增加評估線索：步數需要搭配強度，腿後肌診斷需要考慮其他症狀來源，投球表現需要觀察球種別的時間趨勢。天然產物研究則提醒，機轉資料增加不代表臨床應用已成熟。延續第 34、35 與 37 週的監測與共享決策概念，本週主張先確認資料可比性及功能反應，再討論負荷調整；尚無跨族群通用的風險門檻。 
full-text-web 
依 PRISMA 2020 報告的描述性系統綜述；搜尋四個資料庫，因異質性大未做統合分析。 
26 篇研究中，25 篇為小鼠或大鼠實驗，主要使用力竭運動模型；一篇人體研究涉及健康、未受訓年輕男性的阻力訓練。人體表格列年齡 22–22.6 歲及樣本欄 8/9/10，但未清楚交代各數字對應分組，不能合併成總樣本。 
依來源及化學特性分七類天然產物，包括植物多醣、皂苷、多酚與油脂、複方萃取物、海洋、動物及真菌／發酵來源。 
纳入條件允許安慰劑、空白或陽性對照；部分動物研究另比較成分分離、抗生素處理或糞菌移植。人体抹茶研究使用安慰劑。 
同時報告菌相或代謝物，以及力竭時間、握力、肝肌糖原、疲勞相關生化指標等；人體研究另觀察主觀疲勞、肌力、肌肉量及唾液皮質醇。 
搜尋截至 2026 年 3 月；納入動物介入包括 14 天至 7 週，人體研究為 8 或 12 週，沒有統一追蹤時程。 
證據組成與品質評分 
26 篇研究：25 篇動物、1 篇人體；18 篇（69.2%）Jadad ≥3 分，8 篇（30.8%）低於 3 分。 
作者使用 Jadad 評分，主要失分來自盲法；此評分分布不能消除人體轉譯限制。 
摘要、結果 3.1–3.2 
紅景天苷動物實驗的負重游泳時間 
26.2 分鐘對 10.5 分鐘；p<0.01；未提供信賴區間。 
ICR 小鼠，100 mg/kg、4 週，介入對控制組；屬綜述轉述的單一動物實驗。 
結果 3.3.2 
人體抹茶研究的介入與結果時點 
每次 1.5 g、每日兩次，配合 8 或 12 週阻力訓練；第 1 週主觀疲勞較低，但未提供效應量或信賴區間。 
健康未受訓男性；8 週最大腿部力量增加僅描述為較大趨勢，12 週肌肉量變化較大及皮質醇較低。

檢查決策是否可追溯；流程執行良好不代表已證明降低傷害。 
球速下降可能是值得注意的訊號，但假警報可能造成不必要限制，漏警報也可能讓傷害未被察覺；研究未提供分類準確度。

肩關節囊盂唇傷害：球速下降與修復紀錄，如何改變高需求運動的負荷決策？ 
投手持續掉速，值得啟動評估；肩盂唇完成修復，也仍須追蹤不穩定與實際暴露。本專題串接 MLB 投球追蹤與軍人肩穩定手術研究，建立從訊號查核、臨床交接到受控負荷重建的流程，同時劃清群體關聯、手術結果與個人上場許可的界線。 
sport-medicine 
assessment 
monitoring 
training 
對高需求上肢使用者，何時應把持續的表現下降或修復後不穩感，轉換成負荷調整與肩關節囊盂唇評估？ 
完整閱讀兩篇肩關節囊盂唇研究的研究方法、結果、表格、圖說、討論、限制與所附附錄。MLB 研究提供手術前的表現軌跡；軍人研究提供修復後的失敗定義與結構背景。兩者回答同一決策鏈的不同環節，不能合併估算風險，也不能將軍人修復結果套用為投手 SLAP 手術預後。以下證據等級為本稿對相關結論的編輯判斷，非正式 GRADE 評估。 
本期封包出現投球追蹤、職棒投手盂唇修復與肩部熱身研究題名，顯示肩與上肢議題正受到關注；其中 9 月 11 日的投手盂唇修復題名僅作時效訊號。 
既有負荷專題已強調個人趨勢，但尚未說明：哪些肩部表現訊號有直接研究支持、手術研究如何界定失敗，以及固定材料與骨缺損資訊為何不能替代負荷耐受評估。 
教練、防護員與醫療人員需要共同流程，決定何時查核掉速、何時中止誘發任務、轉介時交付哪些資料，以及完成修復後如何持續監測。 
區分球速、出手運動學、關節內受力與組織診斷。 
正確解讀病例與對照的變化差、每次出賽斜率差及調整後勝算比。 
辨認疼痛、功能受限的不安感與主觀半脫位也可能屬於修復失敗結果。 
建立有負荷紀錄、進退階條件及責任分工的肩部監測流程。 
說明研究未建立的掉速門檻、訓練劑量與回場標準。 
肩部決策須同時理解結構、輸出與暴露。課程提供盂肱關節靜態與動態穩定的基礎；新研究則顯示，外部表現變化與修復後結果各有資訊價值，但它們之間仍缺乏經驗證的個人預測及介入規則。 
關節囊盂唇複合體 
肩關節囊與盂唇所構成的靜態穩定結構，與旋轉肌袖等動態穩定機制共同支持盂肱關節。 
盂唇／關節囊病變與旋轉肌腱撕裂屬不同結構問題；肩痛不能直接指定是哪一種。 
inclass-supported 
出手運動學 
MLB 研究記錄球速、轉速、手臂角度、出手延伸距離及水平／垂直出手位置。 
這些是球與出手附近的外部量測，未直接測量肩部接觸力、肌肉活動或盂唇張力。 
source-stated 
場內逐球變異 
同一投手、同一場出賽、同一球種之量測值標準差。 
低變異代表該指標較一致，不能直接解釋成動作更安全，也不能據此刻意增加投球動作變異。 
時間 × 組別交互作用 
比較病例與對照隨時間改變的差異；最後出賽分析以 mph／次出賽呈現球速斜率差。 
它不是每位病例的實際下降量，也不是可直接套用的停投界線。 
修復失敗 
軍人研究納入再度不穩定、主觀半脫位或脫位、符合不穩定的疼痛、限制功能的不安感，或再次穩定手術。 
失敗範圍比再次手術更廣；沒有再次開刀不等於肩部功能完全恢復。 
勝算比與個人風險 
勝算比描述特定模型中兩組結果勝算的相對關係。 
OR 0.58 不能改寫為每位患者失敗機率降低 42%；還需基準風險、追蹤時間與可比族群。 
cross-source-synthesis 
高輸出與高度一致的投球，可能集中重複負荷 
MLB 病例在前一季有較高球速與轉速，且部分指標逐球變異較低。作者推測重複負荷可能集中於關節囊盂唇局部，但未量測內部受力、組織疲勞或微損傷，亦可能反映不同配速策略。 
【edge-sport-proposal】將這類輸出特徵保留在個人監測背景，不作為降低球速、減重或改亂出手動作的處方。 
pmid-42719368 
輸出下降可能先於外觀明顯改變 
最後出賽窗口的球速斜率出現組間差異，其他平均運動學指標未見顯著差異。疼痛、不穩定或神經肌肉抑制導致輸出下降，是作者提出的解釋，研究沒有直接驗證。 
【cross-source-synthesis】動作外觀穩定不能排除問題；評估應同時納入輸出與症狀。反之，掉速也不能單獨診斷盂唇損傷。 
固定構型與骨性條件提供不同資訊

2010–2020 年現役軍人初次關節鏡肩穩定手術，448 次候選程序中分析前方修復 163 次、後方 51 次、前後合併 111 次。各組年齡中位數約 20.6–21.6 歲，男性占多數；排除上盂唇修復與追蹤不足 2 年者。

把回場決策從單一時間點或單一測驗，改為症狀、能力、運動專項暴露與心理準備的連續判讀。

當運動員的膝痛與腫脹已控制，還需要什麼證據支持回到完整訓練與比賽？ 
共識聲明、臨床指引與前瞻性隊列研究 
回場是一個持續的過程 
Return to sport 不宜只被視為醫療許可；它涵蓋回到參與、回到運動、回到表現三種不同層次，且每一層都需要重新確認風險與能力。 
對稱性是起點，不是終點 
左右側差異可協助發現問題，但仍須放進絕對力量、力量-時間特徵、動作品質與運動專項需求中解讀。 
把競技需求逐步放回復健 
從可控制的力量與跳躍任務，逐步銜接減速、變向、不可預期刺激、密集訓練與比賽節奏，才能觀察身體能否承受真實需求。

變向與減速品質 
訓練後關節反應 
運動員信心與回避行為 
以漸進式全隊訓練暴露取代一次性的通過或失敗判斷。 
把每次測驗連回明確決策：增加、維持或降低哪一種訓練需求。 
同時記錄主觀症狀、客觀能力與訓練暴露，避免只看其中一項。 
與教練、運動防護、復健與營養人員共享當週目標與負荷。 
症狀與關節反應 
它決定後續訓練劑量是否可被組織耐受。 
在關鍵訓練與隔日以相同方式紀錄疼痛、積液、僵硬與活動度。 
力量與力量-時間特徵 
可以分辨完成任務的結果與產生結果的策略。 
選擇信度足夠且團隊能重複執行的測驗；比較個人歷史資料，不只比較健側。 
專項訓練暴露 
比賽需求通常超過單次實驗室測驗。 
追蹤衝刺、跳躍、變向、對抗與訓練密度的進展，以及其後的生理反應。 
期刊趨勢觀察 
回場研究越來越重視『決策品質』與『情境化能力』：絕對表現、動作策略、心理準備與真實運動暴露，通常比單一門檻更能支持跨專業討論。 
Consensus statement 
Ardern CL, et al. 2016 Consensus statement on return to sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern. 
British Journal of Sports Medicine 
提供回到參與、回到運動與回到表現的共同語言。 
Prospective cohort 
Grindem H, et al. Simple decision rules can reduce reinjury risk by 84% after ACL reconstruction: the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort study. 
說明以多項功能與時間條件評估回場的研究脈絡，不應抽離個案背景直接套用。 
Clinical practice update 
van Melick N, et al. Evidence-based clinical practice update: practice guidelines for anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation. 
整合 ACL 復健介入與臨床決策的系統性回顧與共識。 
傷後回場跨領域共享決策：以 ACL Reconstruction 為例 
肌力評估：回到表現

熱環境比賽：讓補水與降溫變成可演練的策略 
把水分、鈉、碳水與降溫策略放進實際賽程和個人流汗特徵，而不是在比賽日臨時猜測。 
nutrition 
monitoring 
performance 
如何將熱、流汗率、補給耐受度與賽事停頓時間轉換成個人化執行計畫？ 
立場聲明、環境生理共識與個人監測 
先量測，再處方 
運動前後體重、攝入液體與排尿紀錄可用於估算流汗率；應在接近比賽條件下重複觀察，才有助於建立可用範圍。 
計畫須經腸胃訓練 
碳水、液體與電解質的攝取策略需要在訓練中反覆演練，並依項目可飲用時機與個人耐受度調整。 
降溫是系統，不是單一產品 
預冷、休息區降溫、衣著、賽中飲品溫度與工作人員流程，應配合運動形式和環境限制整合。 
建立基線 
這位運動員在指定強度與天候下的體重變化和攝入量為何？ 
運動前後體重 
液體攝入量 
尿量與主觀腸胃耐受 
重複測量並保留情境資料，避免以單次數值當作固定處方。 
模擬賽事 
補給與降溫能否在賽事規則和停頓時間內真的完成？ 
可取得補給的時間窗 
裝備與後勤 
腸胃與口感耐受 
將策略放入關鍵訓練或熱適應課表中測試。 
現場調整 
當溫度、濕度、比賽節奏改變時，哪些指標需要重新判讀？ 
RPE 
體重趨勢 
核心症狀與環境資訊 
建立明確的調整與停止運動條件，並遵循賽事醫療流程。 
訓練前後以相同秤重條件紀錄體重與補充量。 
在熱環境訓練中試用比賽日飲食、飲品溫度和補給容器。 
與隊醫和防護人員確認熱傷害辨識、降溫與緊急處置流程。 
體重變化與流汗率估計 
協助描述個人在特定情境下的液體損失範圍。 
將體重、液體攝入、運動時間與排尿量合併記錄，避免只憑感覺補水。 
腸胃耐受與主觀感受 
可執行性和耐受度是策略成功的條件。 
記錄飽脹、噁心、口渴、RPE 與實際完成率，作為下一輪調整依據。 
期刊趨勢觀察 
熱環境研究正從通用補水建議轉向個人流汗、競賽規則、腸胃耐受與後勤流程的整合；安全決策同樣需要把環境與醫療應變納入。 
Position stand 
Sawka MN, et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand: Exercise and fluid replacement. 
Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 
提供運動與液體補充的基礎原則；個人策略仍需依環境與運動型態調整。 
Consensus recommendations 
Racinais S, et al. Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat. 
Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 
整合熱適應、降溫、補水與比賽環境下的實務考量。

從 CMJ 到決策：不要只追蹤跳得多高 
垂直跳高度有用，但若要理解疲勞、訓練適應或傷後策略，還需要看力量-時間特徵、測試條件與個人基線。 
assessment 
monitoring 
training 
同樣的跳躍高度，可能由不同的動作策略產生；團隊該如何避免錯讀資料？ 
統合分析、監測框架與量測方法學 
結果與過程要一起讀 
跳躍高度屬於重要結果指標；若有測力板或可靠的量測流程，離心煞車、向心推進與時間特徵可補足對策略的理解。 
先控制測試噪音 
熱身、手部位置、跳躍類型、測試時間、前一日負荷與資料處理規則不同，都可能讓跨週比較失真。 
用個人趨勢連回訓練脈絡 
單次下降不等於疲勞或風險上升；它需要與主觀恢復、訓練內容、比賽時間表和個人變異一起判讀。 
定義問題 
測試是為了描述表現、恢復、傷後能力，還是訓練反應？ 
決策問題 
可重複的測驗條件 
可用歷史基線 
先寫下測試結果將觸發的決策，再選擇指標。 
建立可靠流程 
每次測試是否以相同方式執行和處理？ 
熱身流程 
量測設備 
跳躍指令與資料篩選規則 
將流程文件化，並定期確認設備與操作者一致性。 
解讀變化 
數值變化是否超過個人正常波動，且與其他資訊一致？ 
個人歷史範圍 
RPE 與睡眠 
近期訓練與賽程 
將資料當作對話起點，必要時重測或補充其他量測。 
固定跳躍協議、鞋款、熱身與測試時段。 
保留原始資料與資料清理規則，讓未來比較可追溯。 
不以單一 CMJ 指標做醫療診斷或單獨決定是否上場。 
跳躍高度與起跳策略 
可提供表現結果和完成方式的不同訊息。 
選擇與目標一致的跳躍任務，搭配一致的資料收集方式。 
力量-時間特徵 
有助於檢視煞車、推進與時間分配是否改變。 
僅追蹤已完成信度評估、團隊能穩定解讀的衍生指標。 
期刊趨勢觀察 
運動科技研究從『收集更多數據』轉向『收集足夠可信、能改變決策的數據』。量測信度、個人基線與資料治理正成為實務重點。

訓練負荷監測：用趨勢管理不確定性 
沒有單一比值能預測所有傷害；真正可用的系統，會把外部負荷、內部反應、可用性與教練情境持續放在一起看。 
monitoring 
training 
sport-medicine 
在賽程、旅行、傷病與球隊戰術不斷改變時，如何讓負荷資料支持而非取代專業判斷？ 
國際共識、系統性回顧與方法學批判 
把負荷視為脈絡資料 
GPS、訓練分鐘數、重訓量、RPE 與睡眠都只描述問題的一部分；必須連回運動員當週可用性、症狀和訓練目標。 
避免只靠單一風險門檻 
急慢性負荷相關方法可協助描述近期變化，但對個別傷害的預測與因果解釋有限，不宜作為孤立的停訓或上場規則。 
讓資料回到教練決策節奏 
每週固定的跨專業短會議，比大量無人解讀的圖表更有機會改變課表、輪替、恢復和傷後進階安排。 
選定最小資料集 
哪些資料足以支援本隊下一週的具體決策？ 
外部負荷 
RPE 或主觀恢復 
傷病與可用性 
從能穩定收集與解讀的少量指標開始，再隨需求擴充。 
辨識有意義的改變 
變化來自訓練設計、比賽、量測噪音還是運動員狀態？ 
週期化目標 
個人變異 
旅行、睡眠與賽程 
先回看暴露與情境，再討論是否需要調整個人或團隊課表。 
記錄決策結果 
資料促成的調整是否改善可用性與表現準備？ 
訓練完成率 
症狀趨勢 
下週回饋 
留下決策理由與結果，逐步建立自己的隊伍知識庫。 
對每個監測指標寫下它回答的決策問題。 
將球隊日程、比賽分鐘數、重訓和復健暴露放在同一時間軸。 
對異常值先確認資料品質和情境，再考慮改變課表。 
外部訓練負荷 
描述完成的跑動、距離、衝刺、跳躍、重量或技術暴露。 
選用與項目需求相符且可持續量測的指標，不比較沒有共同定義的數值。 
內部反應與可用性 
描述運動員對外部需求的生理與主觀反應。 
以 RPE、恢復感受、症狀和出勤狀態等少量高依從性資料建立對話。 
期刊趨勢觀察 
近期方法學討論提醒實務人員：與其尋找萬用傷害預測器，更應建立能及時發現容量、恢復與暴露不匹配的決策系統。 
Consensus statement 
Bourdon PC, et al. Monitoring athlete training loads: Consensus statement. 
International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 
提供內外部負荷監測的共同定義和團隊實務框架。 
Methodological review 
Impellizzeri FM, et al. Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls. 
說明 ACWR 的概念與統計限制，提醒避免把比值變成單一預測規則。 
Review
